name: Creeping push-in
effect: slow-building dread; the audience feels drawn toward something they do not want to see
move: Dolly straight toward the subject at 5-15 cm/s, eye level or slightly below, lens fixed.
rig_notes: Easy for the rail; keep it on one axis so joint speeds stay tiny.
examples: Jaws beach push-ins; Hereditary dinner table

name: Dolly zoom (vertigo effect)
effect: reality warps; sudden realisation or panic while the subject stays the same size
move: Track away from the subject while zooming in (or the reverse) so the subject's framing holds and the background stretches.
rig_notes: Linear move along the camera axis with lens keyframes changing in step; needs a straight track 1-2 m long.
examples: Vertigo bell tower; Jaws Brody on the beach; Poltergeist hallway

name: Steadicam-style follow
effect: relentless pursuit, the viewer is trapped in the space with the character
move: Follow behind the character at a constant distance of 1.5-2.5 m, low height around 0.8-1.2 m, smooth constant speed.
rig_notes: Use the rail's length; long lateral travel. Keep at least 1 m from the actor.
examples: The Shining Big Wheel corridors; It Follows

name: Whip pan reveal
effect: jolt; the audience's attention is snatched to a threat
move: Hold on subject, then a fast pan of 60-120 degrees to the threat in 0.4-0.8 s, settle on it.
rig_notes: Hard for heavy arms: wrist and base joints spike. Ease in for a few tenths of a second and keep the camera position nearly still.

name: Dutch angle drift
effect: unease, something is wrong with the world
move: Slow roll from level to 10-25 degrees while drifting sideways.
rig_notes: Roll is wrist 3; cheap for the arm.
examples: The Third Man; The Exorcist III

name: Overhead god's-eye descent
effect: helplessness; the character is observed by something above
move: Start high looking nearly straight down, slowly descend or rotate.
rig_notes: Straight-down looks are hard for the wrist near the pedestal; tilt 60-75 degrees down instead of 90 and keep 1 m horizontally from the pedestal.
examples: The Exorcist bedroom; Hereditary dollhouse transitions

name: Low-angle menace
effect: the threat towers over the viewer
move: Camera at 0.3-0.6 m height tilted up at the antagonist, slight slow push.
rig_notes: Keep the camera above 0.3 m; the arm needs room under the elbow.
examples: Nosferatu shadow on the stairs; The Babadook

name: Over-the-shoulder lurker
effect: the audience suspects someone is watching from behind
move: Frame the victim from behind a foreground object or over a shoulder, drifting slowly sideways to reveal more.
rig_notes: Lateral rail travel with a fixed look-at point.

name: Slow lateral reveal
effect: suspense; the audience scans the frame for what is hidden
move: Track sideways past a doorway, pillar or furniture so a figure is revealed in the background.
rig_notes: The ideal rail move: mostly the carriage axis, joints almost static.
examples: Hereditary attic; The Conjuring clapping game

name: Snap zoom
effect: shock; a sudden emphasis on a detail
move: Very fast zoom in on a face or object while the camera stays still.
rig_notes: Lens-only; no arm movement at all, so it never violates motion limits.

name: Static locked-off wide
effect: the ghost could appear anywhere; viewers comb the frame
move: No movement. A wide, symmetrical frame held for a long time.
rig_notes: Trivial for the rig; good as an anchor between aggressive moves.
examples: Paranormal Activity bedroom cam; The Shining twins

name: Pull-back isolation
effect: loneliness; the character becomes small and vulnerable
move: Start on a medium close-up, pull straight back and up slightly to a wide.
rig_notes: Back along the rail axis; watch reach when the camera rises at the far end.

name: Orbit / arc around the victim
effect: disorientation; the world is closing in
move: Arc 45-120 degrees around the subject at a constant distance of 1.2-2 m while keeping them centred.
rig_notes: Combine carriage travel with base rotation; keep the radius above 1 m around the actor.

name: Peek around the corner
effect: the camera itself behaves like an intruder
move: Camera starts hidden behind a wall or doorframe and slowly leans out to reveal the room.
rig_notes: Small lateral move plus a slight yaw. Do not intersect the wall prop.

name: Mirror reveal
effect: the jump scare is behind the character, seen in a reflection
move: Frame the character in a mirror; push gently or rack focus as a figure appears behind them.
rig_notes: Keep the camera out of the mirror's reflection line: angle 20-30 degrees off the mirror normal.

name: Under-bed POV
effect: intimate violation; we are the thing under the bed
move: Camera at 0.3-0.4 m looking along the floor toward feet, sliding slowly.
rig_notes: Keep camera above 0.3 m and the forearm clear of the bed box.
examples: The Conjuring; A Nightmare on Elm Street

name: Crane-up reveal
effect: scale; the full horror of the space is revealed
move: Rise vertically 0.8-1.2 m while tilting down, revealing what is behind or below foreground objects.
rig_notes: Vertical reach is limited to about 2 m camera height; stay inside it.
examples: Hereditary treehouse ending; The Shining Overlook exteriors

name: Handheld panic (simulated)
effect: chaos, found-footage immediacy
move: Small, fast, irregular jitters of 2-6 cm on top of a forward move.
rig_notes: Many keyframes 0.2-0.3 s apart with tiny offsets; check acceleration limits.

name: Rack-focus reveal
effect: a figure materialises out of the blur behind the hero
move: Locked or barely moving camera; focus pulls from foreground subject to background threat.
rig_notes: Almost static; lens-only plus a tiny push.

name: Slow tilt-up from feet
effect: dread of what the face will look like
move: Start framing feet or floor, tilt up slowly to the figure's face; camera height constant.
rig_notes: Pure tilt is wrist work; keep the camera at least 1.2 m from the figure.

name: Backward retreat (leading shot)
effect: the character is walking into something only the camera can see behind it
move: Camera moves backward ahead of the walking character, keeping a constant distance.
rig_notes: Long carriage travel; distance to actor must stay above 1 m.
examples: The Shining Danny on trike; Us

name: Corridor symmetry push
effect: inevitability; the end of the corridor is where the horror waits
move: Centred one-point perspective push down a corridor axis.
rig_notes: Line the rail up with the corridor axis.

name: Jump-scare snap-in
effect: maximum jolt on the scare beat
move: Hold still, then a short fast push of 30-50 cm in 0.3-0.5 s timed to the scare beat.
rig_notes: Short distance keeps joint speeds legal; ease in with a keyframe 0.2 s before.

name: Shadow play side light
effect: the threat is a silhouette before it is a body
move: Static or slow lateral move framing a wall where a shadow will appear.
rig_notes: Simple lateral move.

name: Ceiling-corner surveillance
effect: voyeurism; we are watching like the entity does
move: High corner position 2-2.4 m, looking down at 30-45 degrees, very slow drift.
rig_notes: Near the arm's upper reach; keep within about 2 m height.

name: Reverse reveal (turn around)
effect: the threat is right behind the camera's previous view
move: Camera holds on the victim, then rotates 150-180 degrees to show what was behind it.
rig_notes: Large base rotation; give it at least 1.5 s or the base axis exceeds its speed limit.

name: Push through doorway
effect: crossing a threshold into danger
move: Track forward through a door frame into the room, holding centre.
rig_notes: The arm must not touch the door frame props; plan the path through the opening centre.

name: Floating ghost POV
effect: the camera is the ghost, gliding unnaturally smooth
move: Slow, perfectly smooth curving path at head height with a slight vertical bob of 5-10 cm.
rig_notes: This is where a motion-control rig beats a Steadicam: perfectly repeatable for VFX plates.
examples: A Ghost Story; Evil Dead shaky-cam (slow version)
